catalog_quote: The most cognate languages, Katla and Tima, are considered to be tone languages. Therefore, Julut has been analysed with respect to tone. After repeated observations it became clear that tone does not play a decisive role in Julut. In contrast, tone seems to correlate with the feature ATR. ... The phonetic correlate of stress is deemed to be intensity, which is based upon loudness, pitch and vowel length. ... Table 2.15 makes explicit that nouns with [-ATR] vowels and low tone on the first syllable always carry the stress on the first syllable. In other words, the stress pattern of nouns with the value [-ATR] is fairly predictable. The state of affairs is not so straightforward for [+ATR] words. new_statements.quote: Table 2.15 makes explicit that nouns with [-ATR] vowels and low tone on the first syllable always carry the stress on the first syllable. [...] Table 2.16 illustrates that the primary stress falls on the high tone syllable. In HH words, the primary stress is carried by the first syllable if the second syllable is open, but if the second syllable of HH words is closed, it bears the primary stress. [...] In sum, words have their own stress pattern in Julut. This stress pattern corresponds to a presumed tone pattern in which disyllabic LL or LF words carry the primary stress on the first syllable. In other cases, the primary stress occurs with the high tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Julut has word stress (correlate: intensity = loudness + pitch + vowel length) and non-phonemic pitch patterns that track ATR. In disyllables: [-ATR] words (LL/LF pitch) stress the first syllable; [+ATR] words stress the high-pitched syllable (LH -> second, HF -> first); all-high (HH) words stress the first syllable unless the second syllable is closed, in which case the second is stressed. The author frames this as each word having its own stress pattern, i.e. stress is lexically associated but largely predictable from ATR/pitch pattern and final-syllable closure; tone itself is stated to have no phonemic value (p. 46; p. 45: 'tone does not play a decisive role in Julut').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'primary stress' is marked (IPA stress mark) in Tables 2.15-2.16.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 46: 'The tone and stress pattern are not always clear and appear to be different for several words depending on the speaker. The examples in table 2.15 were selected due to their unambiguous results.' Analysis restricted to disyllabic nouns; polysyllables not treated in the preview pages.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, isolated disyllabic nouns (citation forms) elicited from Khartoum-resident speakers; five spectrograms in the book (not in preview) presumably support the intensity claim. Tone analysed with H, L, F labels but declared non-contrastive, so the language is better read as a stress language with ATR-linked pitch than as tonal; reading 'tone language with a stress statement' chosen because the source frames the section as tone-and-stress and neighbours Katla/Tima are tonal — an alternative catalog reading would be 'lexical/weight-sensitive: default initial, final if closed (HH) or high-pitched'.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Julut [julu1237] as spoken mainly by the Khartoum diaspora community (fieldwork 2014-2018 in Khartoum, speakers from all three dialect zones Kujulu / Julut Baca / Kolonggo); author treats Julut as a language separate from Katla [katl1237] (East Katla-Julut dialect continuum per Hellwig). Ethnologue subsumes it under Katla [kcr].

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.4 'Stress and tone' (pp. 45-46): tone is not phonemic (no minimal pairs, speakers unaware of tone; tone correlates with ATR); 'words have their own stress pattern'; disyllabic [-ATR] nouns (LL/LF) always stress the first syllable; in [+ATR] words primary stress falls on the high-tone syllable (LH -> 2nd, HF -> 1st); HH words stress syllable 1 unless syllable 2 is closed, in which case syllable 2 is stressed. Stress correlate = intensity (loudness, pitch, vowel length). Patterns vary by speaker for some words.
